sources.headline: Who are the candidates in Brazil's presidential election?
sources.text: Polls have opened in Brazil to vote for the country's next president. Brazilians are choosing between Brazil's current left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin. Americas correspondent Ione Wells reports from Rio de Janeiro as voters choose between two very different candidates.

sources.headline: Brazil runoff live updates: ballot count resumes after two-hour voting extension
sources.text: From 3h agoVoting time extended for an additional two hoursTom PhillipsScratch that. Brazilian ⁠supreme court justice Cristiano Zanin ⁠has just ordered ⁠voting ​in the country’s presidential runoff ⁠on Sunday to be ⁠extended by ​two ‌hours, granting a ‌request from ‌Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign.Polls were initially set ‌to close at 5pm ​Brasília time. Lula’s campaign ⁠alleged that authorities ​in several cities ​were ​restricting voter ​access ‌to ​public ​transportation.The decision follows allegations of attempted voter suppression in at least 10 states, where public transport appears to have been severely limited in what some suspect was a deliberate ploy to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations.Earlier, Lula told reporters he had never before complained about elections he had been involved in, irrespective of whether he had won or lost. “But this time something abominable is happening.”However, some polling stations may have already closed since the decision came so shortly after they were due to close. People should now be able to vote until 7pm.Key events1h agoPolls close (again) in Brazil runoff election1h agoBattle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensified before presidential runoff2h agoCould highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?3h agoVoting time extended for an additional two hours3h agoPolls close in Brazil runoff election4h agoExclusive: Ex-Lula environmental official warns of Amazon destruction if Flávio Bolsonaro wins presidency4h agoA scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power4h agoLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva v Flávio Bolsonaro: Brazil presidential runoff to decide direction of nationTiago RogeroLula’s main bet in trying to overturn Bolsonaro’s lead was to increase turnout, after abstention reached a record high in the first round – which, according to many polls, disproportionately affected the leftist’s voters, who generally live farther from polling stations.The figures are not yet final, but with 24.4% of polling stations counted, they indicated an abstention rate of 19.38%, down from 21.08% in the first round.Abstention usually rises in Brazilian runoffs – the only exception was in 2022, when the tight contest between Lula and Jair Bolsonaro brought more voters to the polls in the final round.Tom PhillipsMeanwhile, hundreds of Lula supporters have camped out on Paulista Avenue to watch the vote count, which started at 7pm local time.Among them is Camilo Buarque, 35, who came with a bright red banner reading: “Lula: My President”.“I feel so very happy being here and being here fighting for Lula,” Buarque says, predicting his leader will beat Bolsonaro.“My confidence comes from the energy and the happiness and the love of these people [around me]. This is democracy,” Buarque says as the first results come in, giving Lula the lead. Fireworks exploded in the air above him as the crowd celebrated the early lead.João Felipe, a 27-year-old logistics worker, is also there waiting for what he hopes will be a huge Lula party.“I’ve always been poor and Lula was a very important person when it came to helping people improve their lives,” he says.“Lula is going to turn this election around. Long live democracy,” Felipe predicts.“My heart is beating a thousand beats a second but I’m confident,” said his partner, Ester Almeida, 28.A child reacts as supporters of Brazilian president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva gather at Cinelandia to watch the results during the presidential runoff election, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 25 October, 2026. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersTiago RogeroFlávio Bolsonaro is following the count from the mansion of one of his campaign coordinators in a wealthy area of the capital, Brasília. The dozens of journalists present are being kept separate from Bolsonaro and allied politicians, but from time to time they can hear bursts of celebration – like after a goal – whenever the count is updated and Bolsonaro narrows the gap with Lula.When, with 13.65% of the vote counted, Flávio moved just slightly ahead with 50.01%, an AI-generated funk track began playing loudly and the senator’s guests started chanting a line commonly heard in Brazilian football stadiums: “Go at him, Flávio.”And just like that, the race is already tightening further. Bolsonaro now has 50.01% of the vote, while Lula has 49.99% of the vote with just over 13.5% of ballots counted.Tom PhillipsWith 5% of votes counted Lula has taken an early lead with 51% of votes to Bolsonaro’s 48.87%. This is going to be a tight race and a very long night.Journalists work as Brazil resumes the transmission of preliminary election results, during the presidential runoff election, in Brasília on Sunday. Photograph: Mateus Bonomi/ReutersTiago RogeroOne of the most popular figures in Flávio Bolsonaro’s party, congressman Nikolas Ferreira, indicated that the far right could use the extension of voting hours as grounds to challenge the election result in the event of a victory by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Speaking to journalists outside the mansion in Brasília where Bolsonaro was due to follow the count, Ferreira said that “the only person harmed” by the extension was the senator – without, however, mentioning the voters who, as reports throughout the day showed, had been unable to vote because they had no transport.“The extension only helps whoever is losing,” said the 30-year-old politician who, in the first round, became the most-voted federal congressman in Brazilian history, with 3.1 million votes. He added that justice Cristiano Zanin “wanted to disrupt the election” by issuing the ruling.Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, echoed that line and called the justice’s ruling an “intervention”.“I sincerely hope common sense prevails and that any judicial coup or administrative manoeuvre does not succeed, for the sake of democracy,” he posted on social media.Supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro attend an event on the street, waiting for the first results of the presidential runoff election, in Brasília, Brazil, on Sunday. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersPolls close (again) in Brazil runoff electionNow two hours after the initial extension, polls have officially closed in Brazil (save for another surprise extension). Ballot count has begun.Although voting time was extended across the country, some polling stations had already closed by the time that decision was announced. As Brazil uses electronic voting machines, once they are closed, they cannot be re-opened.It’s not clear if certain polling stations had restrictions on if people who arrived after the initial deadline were allowed to vote, as rules usually stipulate that only people in line can still vote after the polls close.The fact that ballot counting was already underway when the polls were suddenly ordered to remain open has led to some confusion and concerns about the integrity of the election results.Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensified before presidential runoffTiago RogeroFive days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.Tom PhillipsLula supporters are starting to gather on Paulista Avenue, at the heart of São Paulo, in anticipation of a Lula victory.The mood is upbeat but tense, amid suspicions that there has been a deliberate pro-Bolsonaro campaign to sabotage public transport systems to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations across the country.Many people on Paulista Avenue outside the iconic São Paulo Museum of Art suspect foul play from Bolsonaro-supporting politicians and business people.“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations. Photograph: Tom Phillips/The Guardian“I’m really worried

 A coin-flip election in Brazil, with little separating the country's left-wing President, Lula, and his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro. The results of the run-off vote will become clear in a few hours.  
 
The contenders have traded insults as they cast their votes, with President Lula describing the choice as one between himself and a morally, ethically and personally unqualified candidate. sources.headline: Brazil: long queues and river journeys mark decisive presidential vote
sources.text:
Across Brazil, voters made their way to polling stations on Sunday 25 October as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faced Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.
In the Amazon rainforest, residents of the isolated Lago do Catalão community travelled by canoe and motorboat to cast their ballots, relying on waterways to access polling facilities.
In Rio de Janeiro's Rocinha favela, long queues formed as residents waited to vote, reflecting the deep divisions surrounding the election.
In Brasília, 59-year-old Cleonice Campos arrived at her polling station holding a small doll resembling President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, keeping it close before casting her ballot in support of the incumbent president.
Brazil's Supreme Court extended voting in the presidential runoff by two hours following complaints that public transport disruptions prevented voters from reaching polling stations.
As voting drew to a close, election officials prepared electronic voting machines and printed electoral rolls. The extended polling period was set to end at 22:00 CET (19:00 Brasília time), with official results expected between 01:30 and 02:00 CET on Monday as vote counting progresses.

SCMP POLL
Igor Patrickin Rio de Janeiro
Published: 5:18am, 26 Oct 2026Updated: 5:55am, 26 Oct 2026

A Supreme Court justice in Brazil ordered polls in the presidential run-off to stay open for two more hours on Sunday, minutes after voting had officially ended at 5pm Brasilia time (4am on Monday in Hong Kong).

The order left election officials across China’s biggest trading partner in Latin America unsure whether to reopen polling stations or send their machines to be counted.

Justice Cristiano Zanin, who was President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s lawyer before joining the court in 2023, acted on a complaint from Lula’s campaign about bus shortages in cities run by allies of his rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.

About an hour later he limited the order to stations whose machines had not yet been shut, so that some voters could cast ballots until 7pm while others were sent home.

The confusion struck an election in which Flavio Bolsonaro is standing in for his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The elder Bolsonaro is barred from office and was convicted by the Supreme Court last year of plotting a coup after losing to Lula in 2022. A week after Lula took office in January 2023, thousands of Jair Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed Congress, the presidential palace and the Supreme Court in Brasilia.

The Superior Electoral Court, which organises Brazilian elections, stopped publishing results at 5.20pm with 0.25 per cent of machines counted. No court had ever prolonged voting in Brazil before.

Voting is compulsory in Brazil, but millions skip it and pay a small fine. Lula built his run-off strategy around getting poorer voters who depend on buses to the polls.

He finished second in the first round this month with 45.16 per cent of valid votes against 47.03 per cent for Flavio Bolsonaro, and no runner-up has ever won a presidential run-off in Brazil.
The race has also turned on Brazil’s ties with Beijing. Lula has courted Chinese investors and backed a trade deal between the Mercosur bloc and China.
A memo carrying Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign branding proposed an anti-China rare earths partnership with the United States, the South China Morning Post reported in September. Flavio Bolsonaro later said he would work with both powers.

Buses kept in depots

The trouble started on Saturday afternoon, when Sao Paulo’s regional electoral court told the city to put its entire bus fleet on the streets for the vote. The municipal transport company said it received the order with less than 12 hours’ notice.

Voters in Salvador, the capital of Bahia state, complained from early morning of long waits and packed buses.

Before lunchtime the head of Bahia’s electoral court had ordered the Federal Police to arrest the city’s mobility secretary, writing that the instruction to cut the fleet had come from his department. He set a fine of 1 million reais (US$197,000) for every hour the order went unmet.

City officials said the secretary was in Paris on an official visit and would return on Monday.

The administration, whose mayor supports Flavio Bolsonaro, blamed the delays on buses covered in campaign stickers, which electoral law forbids. By the afternoon, inspectors from Bahia’s consumer protection agency had counted 544 buses fit to run sitting in five depots.

Sao Paulo, where 9.14 million people are registered to vote and whose mayor also backs Flavio Bolsonaro, had 71.7 per cent of its buses running at 1.20pm according to municipal figures. The Workers’ Party put the figure at 60 per cent. The courts rejected the party’s request to arrest the city’s transport secretary.

Speaking to reporters outside his home in Sao Paulo in the afternoon, Lula called the shortages inexplicable.

“We will not allow robbery, banditry and bandit mayors,” he said.

Flavio Bolsonaro’s lawyers filed their own request after heavy rain, asking for voting to run until 7pm in 17 flooded municipalities in three states.

Electoral court gave 30-minute deadline

Lula’s Workers’ Party and its allies first asked the electoral court to extend voting in Salvador and two neighbouring cities in the early afternoon. At 3.42pm they filed a second petition naming nine more states.

The court’s president Kassio Nunes Marques signed an order at 4.07pm giving Bahia’s electoral court and the electoral prosecution service half an hour to respond.

The deadline expired 23 minutes before polls were due to shut. In the same order he noted that the court had refused to extend voting in the 2022 run-off because the problems reported then had not stopped people from voting. The prosecutors’ reply, which opposed any change to the legal voting hours, arrived at 5.01pm, after voting had ended.

Nunes Marques reached the Supreme Court in 2020 as Jair Bolsonaro’s first appointee and has chaired the electoral court since May.

The electoral court has seven judges, three of them from the Supreme Court, and is always chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Sunday’s dispute therefore pitted two members of the same court against each other.

Nunes Marques has been under pressure for two months over his links to a Banco Master scandal. The central bank shut the lender down last year, and its former owner has been in custody since March.

Files the Federal Police sent to the Supreme Court in September included a contract under which the bank would pay up to 427 million reais (US$84 million) in success fees to a law firm run by the wife of a federal appeals judge. Messages on the banker’s phone placed the judge in a group they referred to by the justice’s initials, KN.

Other messages leaked that month showed the banker authorising monthly payments of 500,000 reais to the Nunes Marques’ son, a lawyer.

In October the local magazine piaui reported that the banker had organised and paid for a party with sex workers for Nunes Marques at his Sao Paulo flat in February last year. The magazine cited messages from the banker’s phone obtained by the Federal Police.

Nunes Marques has denied wrongdoing through his office, adding that he had never voted in the banker’s favour.

Polls already closed when order arrived

By the time the electoral court’s deadline ran out, Lula’s lawyers had already gone to the Supreme Court.

They used a type of complaint that lets parties bypass lower courts when authorities are accused of defying the Supreme Court’s rulings.

Lodged at 4.22pm, their filing accused mayorships of Salvador, Feira de Santana and Lauro de Freitas of breaching a precedent that obliges cities to run free buses at weekday frequency on election days. It asked for voting to be extended nationwide so that all voters would be treated equally.

Zanin, to whom the case was assigned by lot, wrote that the facts had reached the court at 4.32pm. He extended voting by two hours in every polling station in Brazil and left the electoral court to enforce the order, which was issued at about 5.02pm.

Machines had already started transmitting results by then, and at 5.06pm the electoral court published returns from 1,225 polling stations. Poll workers told local newspaper Folha they had received no instructions.

Some had already sent their machines back to regional courts, and the system does not allow a closed machine to be reopened.

Nunes Marques told regional courts in a circular at 5.49pm that only stations still open should keep receiving voters until 7pm. That ruled out reopening closed stations or using paper ballots. The electoral court in Brasilia said it had not had time to apply the extension at all.

Zanin issued a clarification at about 6pm that brought his order into line with the circular. Votes in closed machines would be counted, he wrote, without prejudice to later investigations. He said he had acted on complaints from both campaigns, although Flavio Bolsonaro’s request had gone to the electoral court and was never before him.

sources.headline: Brazil counts votes in presidential runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
sources.text:
Updated on: October 25, 2026 / 6:32 PM EDT
/ AP
Add CBS News on Google
Vote-counting resumed in Brazil's polarizing presidential runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro after voting hours were extended following requests by both candidates for an extension based on issues with voting in their respective strongholds.The extension had caused confusion at many polling stations. Some had already shut down when the decision — made by a Supreme Court justice three minutes before poll close time — was relayed to them several minutes after they'd already shut down, and results were paused until the end of the two-hour window.The decision set the stage for possible legal challenges no matter who wins. Lula's camp said it was already looking into taking legal action because of "interference in the electoral process," said Edhinho Silva, chairman of Lula's Workers Party.Bolsonaro's campaign had yet to comment. Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira is saying the decision that came from the Supreme Court justice, who is also Lula's ex-lawyer, is an attempt to contest Bolsonaro's likely win.The contest will determine whether the U.S. will significantly expand its growing influence in Latin America. A win for Bolsonaro would signify a pivot to the right by Latin America's most populous country and its largest economy, in a year when Trump allies have scored victories in Chile, Peru and Colombia. A victory for Lula would leave Brazil and Mexico with left-of-center leaders.Polls showed the two candidates, who need more than 50% of the vote to become Brazil's next leader in January, in a neck-and-neck race. The election pits the left-of-center veteran politician Lula against Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump and the son of imprisoned former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro.
Voters line up at a polling station during the presidential runoff in Brasilia, Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.
AP Photo/Eraldo Peres
Judge rules to extend voting by 2 hoursAs polls were closing, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled to extend voting nationwide for two hours. The ruling came after both presidential candidates had asked the electoral court to extend voting hours in some cities.
Lula's request came after issues in nine states with buses that provide transportation to polls. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south.In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities.Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. However, more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out.Bolsonaro and Lula have opposing ideological views on issues ranging from U.S.-Brazil relations and climate change to social welfare.
In many ways, Brazil's runoff vote is another tight rematch between the country's two polarized political forces that trigger passion as much as loathing. Four years ago, Lula beat Bolsonaro's father by the narrowest margin since the country's return to democracy in 1985.Security and cost-of-living concernsLula, who first governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010, has faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs.Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.Bolsonaro's admission that he accepted about $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.
Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro and his wife Fernanda Bolsonaro give a thumbs during the runoff presidential election in Rio de Janeiro, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.
AP Photo/Silvia Izuierdo
As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, his supporters shouted "Lula, thief, your place is in prison" while Lula's supporters chanted in his support."The time of real change has arrived," Bolsonaro said. "Brazil can't go on for another four years on its current trajectory."In the lead-up to the vote, Lula frequently portrayed Bolsonaro, whose father is under house arrest for attempting a coup, as a threat to democracy. Bolsonaro has promised to seek an amnesty for his father if elected.
Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives. His government endorsed a debt relief program for small businesses and promised free public transportation on weekends. A major win then came when the Senate backed a popular proposal to end the six-day working week.Lula thanked his voters for an outpouring of support while casting his ballot in the city of Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he began his political career as a union leader in the 1960s. "It is a lot of generosity, a lot of care, a lot of love. I will be forever grateful," Lula said.Lula voters respect his past; Bolsonaro voters want changeLula voters turned out Sunday driven by his history of supporting marginalized people and working to lift Brazilians out of poverty."Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it's like to be poor," Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, said. "I find it impossible not to vote for him."
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection, waves after voting in the presidential runoff in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.
AP Photo/Andre Penner
Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia who sported a red shirt in support of Lula, said he worried about Bolsonaro's long-term political vision, which he called "exclusionary.""It's a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon," he said.Bolsonaro voters, many of whom wore yellow and green Brazil jerseys in support of the senator, said they want change.
"Things are really expensive and taxes are too high," Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said. She added that she once voted for Lula's party but now associates it with corruption.Third-party voters and abstentions from first round could decide voteKelvin Gomes Pimental, a 28-year-old data analyst in Brasilia, voted for a third-party candidate in the first round, making his vote a decisive one in this election. He ultimately decided to vote for Lula."It's not even about Flávio himself. It's also very much about the management of the other Bolsonaro government. He wanted to stage a coup," he said. "These issues scare me a little."Diogo Furtado, a 35-year-old Uber driver in Rio de Janeiro, didn't vote the first time because of his work, but said he'll vote blank on Sunday. He said that neither candidate convinced him."Brazil needs a new candidate," Furtado said. "But unfortunately our country has become dominated by two names: Lula and Bolsonaro."Issues with public transportation affect the voteIn Bahia state, a stronghold for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose voters tend to live in areas that depend more heavily on buses, at least 75 public buses were prevented from leaving municipal garages during the presidential runoff vote, according to a state electoral judge. He ordered the arrest of the mobility secretary of the capital, Salvador, Pablo Souza, in relation to the case.Mayor Bruno Reis, a Bolsonaro ally, blamed trade unionists for illegally sticking Workers' Party materials onto transit vehicles for the measure.
President of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, confirmed that electoral authorities received a report on problems with buses in Bahia that is being analyzed. He did not confirm if voting would be extended, which Lula requested in Salvador and Sao Paulo, where issues with public transportation were also reported in the city with a mayor allied with Bolsonaro."We will not be robbed by mayors, governors or businessmen," Lula told the press. "These people need to respect democracy."Bolsonaro did not immediately comment on the issue.International observers earlier in the day said that voting was occurring peacefully and with transparency and did not immediately comment on the incident.The Trump administration looms largeLula criticized the U.S. president before Brazil's election, speaking about the risks of U.S. intervention in Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports and classified drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations. sources.headline: What are Brazilian voters' main concerns?
sources.text: SAO PAULO, Oct 25 - Brazilians headed to the ballot box on Sunday, in a runoff vote that pits right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.Here are the main themes that have driven the campaign:INFLATIONCost-of-living concerns are widespread. More than two-thirds of respondents told a Quaest poll in August their purchasing power had declined versus the previous year.• Annual inflation stood at 4.58% in the 12 months through September, above the central bank's 3% target, pushing prices — including for food — higher• Lula has pledged to implement measures to allow for steady cuts in borrowing costs and keep inflation under control• Bolsonaro wants to reduce and stabilize public debt to bring interest rates closer to international levels and steer inflation toward the central bank's targetCRIMECrime is another major concern for Brazilians. While Brazil's homicide rate fell by 40% over the last decade, improvements in fighting crime have been uneven, according to the Brazilian Public Security Forum, a think tank.• Bolsonaro has pledged a heavy-handed approach to criminals, promising maximum-security prisons and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses• Lula wants to increase the federal prison system's capacity to hold gang leaders, while still investing in poor areas to reduce the influence of organized crimeCORRUPTIONCorruption is also at the top of voters' minds, with both Lula's circle and Bolsonaro facing scrutiny in high-profile cases.• A major scandal that led to the collapse of mid-size lender Banco Master has sparked multiple probes, including into Bolsonaro over alleged corruption and money laundering, accusations he denies• Bolsonaro has pledged to fight corruption by shielding state-run companies and pension funds from political appointments and expanding transparency in public spending• Lula has vowed to deepen anti-corruption and transparency policies even as his son - who has denied the allegations - is being investigated in probes involving alleged influence peddling, corruption and fraudPUBLIC FINANCESBrazil's public finances are under pressure, especially due to pensions and social benefits. The difficult fiscal outlook has sparked fears of welfare cuts, while many Brazilians are struggling with debt arrears due to years of double-digit interest rates.• Public debt has risen by more than 10 percentage points during Lula's current term, reaching 82.9% of gross domestic product• Brazil's benchmark interest rate of 13.75% remains among the highest in the world• Long-term interest rates fell sharply after Bolsonaro's stronger-than-expected first-round performance• He has promised to ramp up fiscal adjustment, targeting 1.5% of GDP improvement in the primary balance within 18 months to lower borrowing costs• Lula has reiterated commitments to improve Brazil's primary balance targeting an effective surplus near 1.3% of GDP by 2030, versus a projected 0.4% deficit this yearFOREIGN POLICYAfter US President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a swathe of Brazilian goods in 2025, foreign policy became a more prominent issue for many Brazilians.• Bolsonaro has courted Trump and other right-wing allies globally• He wants to rebuild ties with Argentina, the US and Israel, arguing relations with each are close to breaking point• Lula has campaigned for a foreign policy based on multilateralism and stronger ties with the Mercosur bloc of South American states and the BRICS nations• ($1 = 5.0086 reais) REUTERS
